summary:
Western Visayas stands under the national framework of the Philippines, where same-sex relations and trans identity are not criminalised and no provision of national law punishes a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised. There is no administrative legal gender recognition: the Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, a court order is the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress since 2000 without passage, and the protections available to a visitor rest on sub-national and sectoral law: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities, the Magna Carta of Women, the Safe Spaces Act, and Republic Act 11166, which prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression. Of the five provinces in this region, only Iloilo appears in the national inventory of provinces with a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance.

Institutional exclusion on gender-presentation grounds has occurred inside the region. In October 2022 Capiz State University issued a hair-and-uniform directive that excluded students perceived as trans women, and an advocacy campaign followed. A legal-NGO case study dated December 2025 examines that exclusion and its aftermath; the university's binary haircut rules shaped students' everyday conduct, and one graduate reported that cutting her hair in earlier years felt like a loss of self-confidence.

The exclusion did not end in institutional exclusion. At its 21st commencement exercises on 7 August 2025, Capiz State University produced its first openly trans woman to graduate summa cum laude, Khaz-JP Padilla, batch valedictorian of the social work class with the highest Latin honor; reporting attributes the outcome to the advocacy campaign that followed the October 2022 directive. Padilla has described carrying out her transition once pandemic-era online classes freed her from the haircut rule.

For a trans visitor the practical position is legality without a general remedy. Nothing in national law criminalises trans presence or presentation, and a 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall and 62 for trans travellers, within the 'Exercise Caution' band, with 81 for HIV-positive travellers. Refusal of entry or service by establishments, and exclusion from private and public spaces, remains possible with little or no legal consequence where no local ordinance applies.
tangentialFactors:
Local ordinances elsewhere in the Philippines restrict presentation in public: Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. No comparable presentation ban is recorded for Western Visayas in the sources reviewed.

Violence against trans people is documented nationally and recently. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot inside a clinic in General Santos the same day. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas, and in April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage in Bayambang, Pangasinan. Bahaghari cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the SOGIE Equality Bill.

The protection patchwork is uneven by design. Eight provinces with SOGIE ordinances, including Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo, stand against 32 unlisted provinces; sectoral statutes carry their own penalties, among them a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment for SOGIE harassment under the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers, and fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar for slurs and ridicule under the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act.

Detention risk is a standing national concern rather than a documented Western Visayas case: transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories, with head-shaping mandatory on arrival at Manila City Jail and no gender-matched placement, while the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao uses administrative batch transfers of LGBT detainees to a jail annex to prevent abuse.
localsOnly:
For residents of the region, Iloilo is the only Western Visayas province listed among the eight Philippine provinces with a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance. Aklan, Antique, Capiz and Negros Occidental do not appear in that national inventory, and the sources do not record municipal or city ordinances for them.

Capiz State University's October 2022 hair-and-uniform directive applied to students perceived as trans women and was followed by an advocacy campaign documented by a legal-NGO case study dated December 2025. The university's haircut rules operated by sex category, and students described the effect on their confidence and conduct; one graduate described carrying out her transition once pandemic-era online classes removed her from the haircut rule.

The university's 21st commencement exercises on 7 August 2025 were reported by Inquirer.net: Khaz-JP Padilla became the institution's first openly trans woman graduate at summa cum laude, batch valedictorian of the social work class with the highest Latin honor. Reporting attributes the milestone to the campaign that followed the 2022 directive.

Nationally, openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate; the lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist, though Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card in June 2023, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Aklan, Antique, Capiz or Negros Occidental have municipal or city-level SOGI ordinances is not resolved: the national inventory reviewed lists only Iloilo from this region, and absence from that list is not confirmation that none exist.

The current formal status of the Capiz State University hair-and-uniform rule is unresolved. The sources record the October 2022 directive and the advocacy campaign that followed, but do not state whether the university repealed, amended or reissued it.

No visitor-specific violence, arrest or refusal-of-service reporting for Western Visayas was located in the sources reviewed; the risk picture for the region rests on the national framework plus the institutional exclusion documented at one university. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores only Manila, and no equivalent figure for Iloilo City or other Western Visayas destinations is sourced.

The status of the bill permitting markers other than male or female on official documents, filed by trans Filipinos with allies planning endorsement to the 20th Congress on 28 July, is unresolved beyond its non-enactment as of the reports.
